records.story: Rittenhouse began in Philadelphia in 1934, the year after Prohibition ended, when the Continental Distilling Corporation brought out Rittenhouse Square Straight Rye, named, as Heaven Hill tells it, for the city's Rittenhouse Square. Rye had long been the whiskey of Pennsylvania and Maryland, and the label was made to win drinkers back to it. In 1948 Continental dropped Square from the name and remade the whiskey as a four year old bottled in bond. As rye faded behind bourbon, Rittenhouse lived on as a regional label, and in 1993, by Heaven Hill's own history, the Bardstown house took the brand over and made it in Kentucky, to a recipe of 51 per cent rye. Fire destroyed Heaven Hill's Bardstown distillery in 1996; neighbouring distillers made its whiskey under contract until it bought the Bernheim Distillery in Louisville in 1999. By the house's account Rittenhouse was for a time the one bonded rye on the market, and as bartenders went back to the classic rye drinks it became the bottle many of them reached for. Behind a bar it is the working rye of the stirred drink: bonded, 100 proof, and steady in a Manhattan.

records.story: The name goes back to New Orleans, where, by the Sazerac Company's account, a coffee house opened in the French Quarter around 1850 and came to be called the Sazerac Coffee House, after Sazerac de Forge et Fils, a French brandy it imported. Its house cocktail was made with that brandy and Peychaud's Bitters. Thomas H. Handy, who had clerked there, bought the house in 1869 with fellow employees, and his firm grew into the Sazerac Company. As phylloxera ruined the vineyards of France, the story goes, the cocktail turned from brandy to American rye; some historians hold that rye was in it from the start. The company bought the Frankfort distillery in 1992 and renamed it Buffalo Trace in 1999, and in 2006 it launched Sazerac Rye in a bottle modelled on the house's packaging of the 1880s. In 2008 Louisiana named the Sazerac the official cocktail of New Orleans, and in 2025 the distillery set a 100 proof and a 125 proof version beside the 90. For a bartender it is the rye that shares its name with the drink, and the plain answer when a guest asks what goes in a Sazerac.

records.story: The name is that of Thomas H. Handy (1839 to 1893, as the Sazerac Company gives his dates), who went to work as a clerk at the Sazerac House in New Orleans. In 1869, by the company's account, he and several fellow employees of his firm, Thos. H. Handy & Co., bought the house, and the Sazerac Company grew from that firm. By the company's telling it was in his time that the Sazerac cocktail came to be made with American rye in place of French brandy, as phylloxera ruined the vineyards of France. More than a century later the company's Frankfort distillery, Buffalo Trace since 1999, began its Antique Collection in 2000, and Thomas H. Handy joined it in 2006 as the rye bottled straight from the barrel, uncut and unfiltered, beside the 18 year old Sazerac. For its first twenty years the barrels were mostly around six years old; with the release of 2026 the distillery set a floor of twelve years for every barrel. For a bartender it is the Sazerac rye at full strength: read the proof off the label, and pour it with water at hand.

records.story: The name is that of Pikesville, a town outside Baltimore, and by Heaven Hill's account the rye was first made in Maryland in 1895, when Maryland, like Pennsylvania, was rye country. Prohibition all but ended Maryland's rye trade. Pikesville came back after Repeal and, as Heaven Hill tells it, held on as the last Maryland rye standing. In 1982 Heaven Hill of Bardstown bought the brand, and once distilling in Maryland had ended it made the whiskey in Kentucky. For more than thirty years Pikesville lived on mostly in Maryland, as a young rye at 80 proof. In 2015 Heaven Hill relaunched it as a six year old straight rye at 110 proof, distilled at its Bernheim Distillery in Louisville and aged at Bardstown, and the young rye went on, on Maryland shelves, as Pikesville Supreme. The house's rye recipe also makes Rittenhouse, so the two can be poured side by side to show what the extra years and ten more proof do. For a bartender it is the bridge between two rye traditions: a Maryland name with Kentucky whiskey in the bottle.

records.story: Michter's traces its line to a distillery near Schaefferstown, Pennsylvania, where, by the brand's account, Swiss Mennonite farmers of the Shenk family began distilling rye in 1753. The site later passed to the Bomberger family, and in the 1950s an owner named its whiskey Michter's, joining the names of his two sons. In 1980 the old Bomberger's Distillery was made a National Historic Landmark. The business went bankrupt in 1989, the Pennsylvania distillery closed soon after, and the name was left to lapse. In the 1990s two men from the drinks trade bought the trademark and rebuilt Michter's in Kentucky, bottling at first whiskey bought from other distillers, then whiskey others distilled to its own specification. By its own account the house bought a building at Shively in Louisville in 2011, and in August 2015 it began filling barrels of its own whiskey there. The US*1 Rye, bottled one barrel at a time below the strength of the bonded ryes, became the rye guests ask for by the Michter's name. For a bartender it is the gentle side of Kentucky rye: single barrel, low in proof, and an easy first rye to pour.

cards.answer: A distillery near Schaefferstown, Pennsylvania, whose owner in the 1950s joined the names of his two sons.

quiz.q: A guest finds bonded rye too hot and asks for Michter's US*1 Rye. At what proof is it bottled?
quiz.explain: It is bottled at 84.8 proof, 42.4% ABV; 100 proof is the strength of the bond, which Rittenhouse carries.

quiz.q: Michter's takes its name from a distillery in which state?
quiz.explain: The name was first given to the whiskey of a distillery near Schaefferstown, Pennsylvania, in the 1950s; Kentucky is where the house rebuilt it.

report: The plan's question of the still is settled only in part: Michter's bought its Shively site in 2012 and was distilling all its own whiskey by 2015 (VinePair, and a Sotheby's article on the house); earlier whiskey was sourced and then contract distilled from about 2003 (VinePair). Michter's own pages do not say which rye bottlings came from which still, so the record says both and names no contract distiller.
The mash is unpublished; the 53, 33, 14 of one retailer is left out as the plan asks.

The two men who bought the trademark are left unnamed: sources name both, and both belong on people.json's names list (Joseph Magliocco, Dick Newman); this task may change only the fragment, so the integrator should add them. The 1950s owner and his two sons are also left unnamed; none is known to have died with two sources.

Sources differ on the purchase of the trademark (1996, 1997 or the late 1990s) and on the closing of the Pennsylvania distillery (1989 in Wikipedia, February 1990 in VinePair and a writer's history): the record says the business went bankrupt in 1989 and the distillery closed soon after, and the 1990s for the trademark.

The 1753 founding is the brand's claim for an ancestor and is told as such; year is left empty for that reason. The National Historic Landmark of 1980 rests on Wikipedia and the National Park Service nomination.

Left out for want of a second source: the Fort Nelson distillery and its old Pennsylvania pot stills (Whisky Advocate alone), the barrel entry proof of this rye (Michter's tour pages give 103 and 125 for two single barrel ryes without saying which), heat cycled warehouses, and the meaning of US*1.
The Library's Michter's record gives a barrel entry proof of 103 and heat cycled warehouses as house practice; neither was confirmed for this bottling, so neither is used. Its wording was not copied.
The roster prints US*1 with an asterisk; the label prints a star, which the voice refuses, so the asterisk stands throughout.

changed: bottle.still and story: the Shively building was bought in 2011 by Michter's own account (2012 in Whisky Advocate), and barrels were first filled there in August 2015 (Whisky Advocate, The Daily Beast); now says so, where it said bought in 2012.

bottle.still and story: that by 2015 the house distilled all its own whiskey is cut to the date it began filling barrels; bottles on a shelf after 2015 held older bought or contract whiskey for some years.

story: contract distilling from about 2003 rested on VinePair alone and is cut; now says the house bottled at first whiskey bought from other distillers, then whiskey others distilled to its own specification.
open: story: the 1950s owner who named the whiskey for his two sons is in Tasting Table, VinePair and others; one account gives 1942 for the first use of the name. The owner and his sons stay unnamed.
story: the year the trademark was bought is given as 1996, 1997 or the mid 1990s; the record says the 1990s.
bottle.wood: no age statement, but the house gives no age either; nothing is said of one.
